_note: Style presets, ported from the old tool's niche_styles.json.
niche     - subject matter and tone (WW2 History, True Crime, Relationship Advice)
art_style - how the picture is rendered (Studio Ghibli Style, Pixar 3D, Chibi Cute)
style - the STYLE: line in the agent prompt (story_to_agent_prompt.js)
whisk - wording for character-sheet / image prompts, used by hand in Whisk
The rest - palette, camera, audience - are authoring notes for a human. No tool
`label` MAY NAME A REAL STUDIO. `style` and `whisk` MUST NOT.
The label is a menu entry; the other two are typed into a prompt. Naming a real
studio or brand is a distinctive protected house style, and Google's models
often refuse or quietly sanitise such prompts. The Bridge story had to be
rewritten to remove 27 mentions of one studio name for exactly this reason, so
the presets describe the look instead. Label 'Studio Ghibli Style' is how you
find the entry; its `style` says 'hand-painted 2D animation, soft watercolour
backgrounds' and never uses the word. Swap a label's wording into `style`
yourself if you would rather name the studio and take the risk.

ANIMALS: the exact breed or mix, natural build and size, real fur with individual strands visible, correct eye colour, and two unchanging physical markers. styles.direction: Ground every animal in real behaviour - head turns, ear tilts, weight shifts, shivering, a vigilant stance, cautious hesitation. An animal is never a passive prop and never behaves like a person. Humans are ordinary and tired, never villains and never saints. Put a hook - a visual anomaly or a striking emotional beat - inside the first two seconds. Deliver the lesson through action and through what it costs, never by saying it.

styles.label: Geography Map (2.5D relief)
styles.style: Dark-mode 2.5D topographic shaded-relief cartography, satellite-photoreal hybrid, exaggerated 3D elevation casting long shadows, glowing luminous neon vector boundaries, volumetric atmospheric lighting, deep-space vignette at the frame edge, premium technical infographic finish, zero on-screen text, ultra-sharp 4K satellite aesthetic, NOT flat 2D vector art, NOT toy-like, NOT cel-shaded
styles.whisk: Dark-mode 2.5D topographic relief map, satellite photoreal hybrid, exaggerated elevation, glowing neon boundaries, volumetric lighting, deep-space vignette, zero on-screen text
styles.palette: Deep Midnight Ocean #080C16, Charcoal Slate Terrain #1C222D with shaded ridges #2A323D, Luminous Amber Gold highlight #FFB703, Electric Neon Cyan waterways #00E5FF, Laser Crimson divider #FF2A42, Lowland Moss Green #2A4736
styles.camera: Relentless kinetic motion, 9:16 vertical: high-angle orbital satellite dives, 45-degree isometric flyovers, low-altitude tracking drifts along coastlines and lines. Never a locked-off static shot. Smooth ease-in/out landing on a landmark, rapid zoom-dives through cloud layers, match-cuts on colour fills, whip-pans along neon vectors.
styles.direction: Every clip is an evolving geographic VISUALISATION, not a flat slide: glowing boundaries, dashed tracer lines with animated chevron arrows, and translucent illuminated polygon fills demonstrate the single factual claim the narrator is voicing at that instant. Frame ONE already contains the anomaly: the surprising visualisation is happening in the first second - never a slow map tour, a zoom-out to establish, or any build-up. Clip 1 is a HOOK and never the first fact: lead with the single most counter-intuitive claim as a flat STATEMENT, not a question (a question is only the fallback). Every clip after carries exactly ONE new fact or deduction with its specifics (a length, a year, a country, a number) and never repeats the previous line. The last clip is the biggest revelation and its final frame visually echoes the first frame so the film loops. Show the fact, never narrate a walkthrough. Exaggerate every instruction - the model treats 'moves' as 'barely moves': say fast, aggressive, big dramatic framing change, never static. Numbers are spoken as words ('seven thousand', not '7,000'). No people, no talking heads, no on-screen text.

styles.direction: This is a two-hander. Two people are together in one calm, beautiful room and talk to each other - the SAME room and the same light for the entire film. They never move to another place and the room never changes. Nothing about either of them changes either: the same face, the same hairstyle and the same clothes from the first clip to the last. Everything said is said out loud by one of them to the other, in their own voice. There is no narrator and nobody describes the scene. Build the exchange as a hook that makes the viewer stop, then two or three numbered rules, then the younger one pushing back with the doubt the audience is actually feeling, then one sharp aphorism worth repeating, then a warm resolution. Give the listener something to do while the other speaks: a hand stilled, a shoulder turned away, an eye-line that drops and comes back. The camera cuts to whoever is speaking: when one of them talks, the shot is an over-the-shoulder close-up framed on the speaker with the listener in soft focus in the foreground; when both speak, or a beat needs air, hold the wide two-shot. Cut between angles, never pan, and keep the same axis so their left and right positions never flip. Let the warmth be earned by the truth of the advice, never by sentimentality.
styles.blocking: SPATIAL BLOCKING (LOCKED): the character laying down the rules holds the screen-LEFT position, angled facing right, and keeps it for the whole film. The character hearing them holds screen-RIGHT, angled facing left, and keeps that too. Whether the story has them seated or standing, they never swap sides, never leave the frame, and the camera never crosses the axis between them. Neither of them changes clothes, hairstyle or jewellery between clips - the face and the wardrobe in clip 1 are the face and the wardrobe in the last.
